title: devbin release core: one shared release sequence for every project that releases, devbin its first user
objective:
Ship a release core in devbin: the one sequence every releasing project runs, so no project writes its own orchestrator again. The core covers pre-flight, version stamping, dating the notes, the commit, the gates on the release commit, the one confirmation, the annotated tag, the per-remote push and the release object, each step reading its own postcondition so a re-run continues. Each project keeps its own parts: its version files, its CI build, its packaging such as a Homebrew formula.

Design first. No code lands before the design is reviewed.

devbin is the core's FIRST USER, not Utilz (hv, decision 26, 2026-09-16): the design is not finished until devbin's own release is expressible in it without a devbin-only branch, including the half devbin's CI already owns. devbin cut v0.1.2 that way on 2026-09-19. Utilz, then Conflab, then Intent adopt afterwards (WP-08). The thread's title was written before that ruling and named Utilz as the first user; it now names devbin.
context:

The thread was minted on 2026-09-16 by vc, on hv's go. hv then ruled that devbin adopts first (decision 26): the design is not finished until devbin's own release is expressible in it without a devbin-only branch.

Three projects already carry their own orchestrator for this sequence: Intent (1,170 lines), Intentv2 (839, a fork of Intent's) and Conflab (399), 2,408 lines between them. Devbin's own `release` command was the notes half only. devbin ships `version`, and that is the one piece of the sequence all of them share. cc's research is at `intent/whiteboard/cc/.history/20260914/0064-release-orchestrator-research.md`. Utilz's requirements are in 0064: the tag name is the project's, annotated tags need `--cleanup=whitespace`, CI must be green on the commit being tagged, and `--help` never cuts a release. Utilz's own parts are in Utilz's ST0019, drafted by utilz-cc and reviewed by utilz-vc.

As built, to 2026-09-21: WP-01 to WP-07 are done and 0064 is closed. devbin 0.1.2 ships the core and was cut with it -- `bin/devbin release v0.1.2`, tag at `df56014`, the GitHub release made by devbin's own workflow under `object: ci`. The cut's own gate on the release commit found and stopped a test defect before anything was tagged, which is the ordering the core exists to guarantee. The 0.1.2 sweep then put that runtime into 14 estates; Laksa alone is still held for its own window. devbin 0.1.3 (fixes 0094, 0095, 0096) was cut the same way on 2026-09-21 -- `bin/devbin release v0.1.3`, tag at `54416d5`, every step done or skipped -- and its fleet sweep waits on hv's go. wps.title: The release schema, opt-in activation, release check's declaration half, and the argument loop
wps.objective: Give the release core its declaration and its front door before any step exists. An opt-in `release` catalogue row (D35). The `release:` schema, one table in `lib/config` with a default for every key, refusing a key the declared mode never reads (D37). `release check`'s declaration half, and doctor's note on a block nothing reads. wps.title: release status: every step's postcondition, read-only -- the resume map
wps.objective:
`release status <target>` answers where a release has got to, by reading each of D38's eleven rows and nothing else, and it writes nothing at all.

**The postcondition readers are the deliverable; the printout is what they are first used for.** Every step of a cut asks "has this already happened?" before it acts, and that question has exactly one answer per step. WP-04 onwards call these readers to decide whether to act, and `release status` calls the same ones to report. **Two readings of one postcondition -- one that decides and one that reports -- is how a resume map comes to disagree with the resume it claims to describe**, and the disagreement would show up as a status that says `already` while the cut runs the step again, or worse the other way round. The worked case is already visible: pre-flight's "when the tag exists, its commit must carry step 3's result, else REFUSE" is step 4's postcondition read at a different moment, so it is one reader serving a report and a refusal.

**ELEVEN ROWS, FIVE POSTCONDITIONS, and this sentence said eleven of each until the reading was done.** Steps 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 carry something the repository can be asked. Steps 1, 2, 10 and 11 carry none, and steps 5 and 6 carry a predicate over OTHER rows' readers rather than one of their own -- which is the whole reason they must not grow a second reading of "has the push happened".

**Read-only in the strong sense, and proven that way rather than argued.** Nothing in the working tree, no ref, no remote and no release object changes. The test compares the whole repository state either side of a run -- `git status --porcelain`, every ref, and the remotes' answers -- rather than reading the code and concluding it writes nothing. `.git` itself is deliberately outside that claim: `git archive` on an LFS project downloads objects and writes `.git/lfs/objects`, measured, so a test asserting `.git` is byte-identical would be asserting something false about a project devbin supports.

**FOUR STATES, and the fourth comes from the declaration rather than from the repository.** `already` and `pending` are what a postcondition answers. `not re-run` is the third and is not a softer second: past step 7 the gates cannot honestly re-run and cannot honestly claim to have passed, because a tag the core reuses may never have been gated by this core at all, and step 6 reaches it only when no irreversible step has work left. **`skipped` is the fourth** (principle 4, "declared off"): step 9 under `object: none`, step 10 with no `after:` and step 11 with no `ci.query` have no postcondition and never will, so reporting them `pending` would promise a run that will not happen.

**A fact the run cannot reach is reported as unreadable, never as false.** A remote whose `branch` head is a commit this checkout does not hold cannot be tested for ancestry, and status may not fetch, because a fetch writes refs. Git already separates the two -- `merge-base --is-ancestor` exits 1 for a genuine non-ancestor and 128 for a sha it does not have, measured -- and the reader keeps them apart, for the same reason `lib/release.notes` keeps "found it stale" and "could not look" on different statuses.

**It carries the materialiser WP-02 deferred.** Every notes verb takes the root it reads and no answer depends on anything else, so asking about a commit means materialising that commit's WHOLE tree and naming it as the root -- whole, because `notes_paths` is what a release owns rather than what a verb reads. WP-03 builds that materialiser and declares its limits, which is the half WP-02 named and left. It materialises under `$TMPDIR` and never under the project root, because a materialised tree inside the working tree is untracked non-ignored dirt -- exactly what step 4's cleanliness clause reads -- so a status run would change the fact it reports.

**The release commit is HEAD while no tag for the target exists, and the tag's commit once it does.** Status reads it that way, so a finished release re-read after HEAD has moved on names the commit that was tagged rather than refusing or reporting the wrong bytes. Two clauses follow from that definition and are written down because they are easy to get wrong: step 7's "and points at the release commit" cannot fail once the tag exists and is therefore not a check, and step 4's "the tree is clean" holds only while the tag is absent, or a released project with ordinary work in progress would report its own release commit as uncommitted.

wps.title: Steps 1 to 5 with --dry-run: resolve, pre-flight, stamp, commit, gates on the release commit
wps.objective: Build the first five steps of a cut -- resolve the version, pre-flight, stamp, make the release commit, and run the gates on it -- with --dry-run, so a cut stops safely before anything outward happens.

wps.title: Steps 6 to 9 for object local and none: confirm, annotated tag, per-remote push, release object
wps.objective: Build steps 6 to 9 of a cut for object local and none -- one confirmation naming everything other machines will see, an annotated tag at the release commit carrying the note's body, a push of only what each remote lacks, and the release object made or brought to this release's title and notes -- each reading its postcondition first, so a cut that stops anywhere resumes, and a tag is never moved.

wps.title: object ci with object_wait, and step 11's CI verdict after the release
wps.objective: Under object: ci the core makes no release object and waits up to object_wait for the project's workflow to make one; under a declared ci.query it asks the verdict on the tagged commit after the release, and anything but green exits 1 with the fail-forward remedy, leaving the tag and the release as they stand. Every call to another machine from the first push on is bounded, and a bound kills the whole call.

wps.objective: devbin releases itself with the release core: its release: block declares the releases notes kind, object: ci, its repository and doctor as a gate, docs/releasing.md is the human steps and bin/devbin release, and devbin 0.1.2 was cut that way on 2026-09-19.

release status <version> reads every step's postcondition and prints the table a cut's summary prints, writing nothing to the tree, the refs, any remote or any release object.

Asking a notes verb about a commit materialises that commit's whole tree, its own bytes, at a root outside the project and removes it on every exit path including a refusal, so a status run cannot alter the dirt it reports; the tree is written from an index of its own rather than by git archive, so no export attribute can drop or rewrite a path and make a correct release read as unstamped or its views STALE, and the limits that remain -- smudge filters and submodules -- are declared.
Every step's failure is a non-zero exit naming the step, held by a test per step with that step's command stubbed to fail.

The gates run on the release commit, and the core checks that they did: a gate reading a file only the stamp writes passes and fails if the gates move before step 3; an untracked non-ignored file outside the owned set is refused at pre-flight; a gate that writes or creates a path fails step 5 naming it.
While the tag is absent, pre-flight refuses a dirty path outside the owned set and names it, and step 4 commits a dirty path inside it, whether a human or a killed run wrote it.

Pre-flight refuses, naming the remote, when a remote's branch neither contains the release commit nor is an ancestor of it, before any gate runs; a remote whose branch has moved past the release commit passes with its push already, once that commit exists; while the release commit is still to be made on HEAD, a remote whose branch has moved past HEAD is refused too, since the commit step 4 makes would diverge from it.
A tag for the target whose commit does not carry the release (VERSION is not the target, or the note is not dated for it) is refused and never moved or deleted.
--dry-run writes nothing and names every refusal it could not reach.

A release killed after each of steps 3, 4, 7 and 8 is completed by re-running the same release <target>, no step whose postcondition held runs twice, and the gates run again on every resume before the tag exists.

A finished release re-run after HEAD and every remote have advanced, with work in progress in the tree, reports every step without refusing, runs no gate (step 5 not re-run), asks nothing (step 6 not re-run), and pushes nothing.

A release resumed after step 7 with pushes outstanding prompts before the first push, naming only the remaining pushes and the object; without a tty and without --yes it exits 2 having pushed nothing.

A tag the core makes is annotated, at the release commit, and its message is the notes body byte for byte, ### lines included; a tag the core reuses whose message differs, or which is lightweight, is reported on step 7's line and left as it is.

Under object: local the core makes exactly one release object, titled from title:, and a resume edits it rather than making a second, only when its title or notes differ from this release's and only in a confirmed run: an unconfirmed run names the difference and changes nothing; release status reads the same, row 9 already only when the object carries this release's title and notes; under object: none it makes none.
Under object: ci the core makes no release object, and step 9 reports done only when a release object exists for the tag within object_wait, never on a CI verdict for the commit.
Under a declared ci.query, a red verdict on the tagged commit exits non-zero, names the run and states the fail-forward remedy, and leaves the tag and the release untouched.

# ST0007 Design: the devbin release core

**Drafted by `devbin-dc` on hv's ruling of 2026-09-16 18:00Z, relayed by vc: dc writes the design, vc reviews it, and nothing is built before that review.** Every decision below is PROPOSED unless marked RULED. hv ruled on v0.1's four questions on 2026-09-16 (hv decisions 26 and 28; see "hv's rulings" at the end). **v0.3 applied vc's review of v0.1 (seven findings) and vc's two notes on v0.2. vc approved v0.3 with two findings to fold (S1, S2) and two minor ones (M1, M2), and v0.4 folded all four. vc approved v0.4 with N1 and N3 to fold and N2 at dc's judgement; v0.5 folds all three**, and the ACs are minted from it. "What changed, finding by finding" at the end maps each to where it landed. What remains open is the utilz-cc questions.

This document does not restate that survey. ## What the core is for, in one paragraph

Three projects each wrote the same sequence -- resolve a version, pre-flight, stamp, date the notes, commit, tag, push, make the release object -- and the copies disagree about safety (R-B): one leaves its commit, tag, pushes and `gh` call unchecked and cannot resume after a partial failure, one moved an existing tag, and devbin's hand procedure re-dated a note after its tag. **The core is the one copy of that sequence, and the properties each copy lacks are the core's policy, not options a project sets**: every step's exit status is checked, a failure part-way leaves a state the next run continues from, `--help` in any position never acts, the gates examine the commit that is tagged, and a tag whose commit does not carry the release it names is refused rather than moved. What differs between projects is declared as data (R-E); what is the same is not declared at all.

## Principles

1. **The sequence is the core's; the facts are the project's.** A project declares its tag template, where its notes live, its gates, its remotes, and who makes the release object. It never re-orders, skips or re-implements a step. A project that needs a step the core lacks gets a hook at a named point, never a fork.
2. **Every step checks its postcondition first, so a re-run continues.** The state of a release is read from the repository and its remotes -- VERSION, the note's status, the commit, the tag, each remote's refs, the release object -- never from a state file the core writes. Two sources for one state is the drift this project keeps finding; a state file is also exactly what a crashed run leaves wrong.
3. **Nothing irreversible happens before every reversible thing has passed, and before the one confirmation.** Reading, stamping, committing and gating come first, then the confirmation. The first act another machine sees is a push, and it happens only after the release commit is gated, the human has confirmed, and the tag is made and verified.
4. **A step that did not happen is never reported as done.** The summary names each step as `done`, `already` (its postcondition held on arrival), `skipped` (declared off), or `FAILED`, and the run's exit status is non-zero if any step failed. `--dry-run` reports `would`, and a refusal that `--dry-run` cannot reach is named as such rather than implied to have passed (R-B: Intent's dry run silently passes refusals only a real run meets). **A step with no postcondition the repository can show -- the gates, the confirmation -- is never `already`.** The gates run again until the tag exists, and past it report a fifth state, `not re-run`, which says only that they did not run and why (D38), never that they passed. The confirmation runs again whenever an irreversible step still has work left, however far a previous run got.
5. **devbin is a user of its own core, and adopts it first** (hv, 2026-09-16, decision 26). The design is not finished until devbin's own release is expressible in it without a devbin-only branch, including the half devbin's CI already owns.
6. **No project is a special case** (hv, 2026-09-16, decision 26). Every project that releases adopts the core the same way, through its `release:` block; a difference that a block cannot express is a missing key in the core, not a branch for one project. The one exception is ruled rather than chosen: Intentv2 is frozen.
7. **Every key has a default, and every default can be overridden** (hv, 2026-09-16, decision 26). A project declares only where it differs.

## The shape

### D35 -- A builtin, `release`, in the Ship group, spelled the way the fleet already spells it, and opt-in. RULED (hv: follow the existing pattern; opt-in, taking vc's recommendation)

**How it is done elsewhere, read from source on 2026-09-16.** Of the release commands in the fleet, two are top-level `release` (devbin's `cmd/release`, Conflab's `cmd/release`) and one is an arm of `build` (Intent's `build.d/release`, with Intentv2's fork of it). Every one that cuts a release takes the same arguments: a required `--patch`, `--minor`, `--major` or `vX.Y.Z`, with `--dry-run`, `--help` in any position, and a bare invocation that prints usage and exits 1. The ones that do more than cut add NAMED sub-verbs beside the target -- devbin's `notes` and `check`, Conflab's `list`. Outside the fleet the verb is the same: `cargo release`, `goreleaser release`, `gh release`. **So the core is a top-level builtin `release`, taking that argument shape.**

**It is `opt-in`, exactly as `publish` is** (`lib/builtins`: `publish opt-in - - Ship`). Most of the 16 estates never release, and with every key defaulted (principle 7) an `any` row would make `release` appear in every one of them, and be runnable there. A project enables it the way it enables any opt-in builtin, `commands.release.enabled: true`, and no second activation route is added: a `release:` block does NOT enable the command by being present, because that would be a new activation rule for one row. **A `release:` block in a project that has not enabled `release` is reported by `doctor` as declared and inert**, since inert configuration otherwise says nothing.

The row is `release opt-in - - Ship @builtin`, vendored with the runtime. A project that spells it `build release` declares that arm as `run: bin/devbin release`, so ST0019's `dvb build release` keeps working for Utilz, as does Intent's.

**A new builtin is a fleet-blast-radius change, and the pre-notice reservation applies** (standing directive 11 exempts only guard bodies resolved live out of `INTENT_HOME`). The sweep that first carries `release` to the estates is announced before it runs. Being opt-in, it changes nothing an estate can run until that estate enables it.

**Shadowing, and every project with a `cmd/release` meets it the same way.** A project handler shadows a builtin totally (doctor announces it, 0024), so a project's own `cmd/release` hides the core. Adopting the core means deleting that handler, for devbin and for every other project alike. devbin's is deleted in WP-02, when its notes generator moves into the core (D39).

### D36 -- The command line. PROPOSED, in the shape D35 found

| Invocation                                                | Writes           | Does                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `release <--patch\|--minor\|--major\|vX.Y.Z> [--dry-run]` | everything below | Cuts the release: runs the sequence from the first step whose postcondition does not hold.                     |
| `release status <vX.Y.Z>`                                 | nothing          | Reads every step's postcondition for that version and prints the table a cut's summary prints. The resume map. |
| `release notes`                                           | the notes views  | Regenerates the notes views, where the notes provider has any (D39).                                           |
| `release check`                                           | nothing          | Predicate: the notes views match their source, and the `release:` block is well-formed.                        |
| `release` (bare)                                          | nothing          | Usage, exit 1.                                                                                                 |

**The target decides the bump, so no key does.** `--patch`, `--minor` and `--major` compute the next version from the newest tag matching `tag:` and stamp it. An explicit `vX.Y.Z` (the `v` is optional) is that version: when VERSION already says it, the stamp is `already` -- devbin's documented rule that the bump is the human's decision, expressed as the human naming the version -- and otherwise it is stamped. **Either way the target must exceed the newest matching tag other than its own** (its own existing is a resume, D38), not VERSION, because after a stamp or under a human-written VERSION they are equal (R-B: a resume refused for exactly this reason). **`--dry-run`** runs every read and every gate and prints each write as `would`; because the gates run on the release commit (D38 step 5), a dry run gates the current HEAD, says so, and names the result as a prediction about a commit it did not make. **Every argument is parsed before any action**, and `-h`/`--help` in any position prints usage and exits 0 (R-B; 0064's `macos prepare --help` rebuilt Intent.app).

### D37 -- The project's declaration: one `release:` block in `bin/.devbin/config.yaml`, every key defaulted. PROPOSED (the defaults RULED in principle by hv)

Each key is justified by an observed difference between projects (R-E), and each has a default (principle 7). **A project that has enabled `release` (D35) and declares no `release:` block cuts a release with every default below**; a block names only what differs.

```yaml

  tag: "v{version}"            # R-E1. Most tags carry a `v`; Utilz overrides with "{version}".
  remotes: []                  # R-E8. Empty means every remote `git remote` lists, in that order.
  branch: main                 # every project releases from main.
  notes:                       # R-E2, R-E3.
    kind: changelog            # changelog | releases | command. A `## [X.Y.Z]` CHANGELOG section is the common shape.
  derived: []                  # R-E5. Commands that regenerate derived files, each printing the paths it wrote.
  gates: [check all, test all] # R-E6. devbin verbs every project has, run in order on the release commit; each must exit 0.
  ci:                          # R-E7. Absent means CI is not consulted.
    query: ""                  # a command printing green | failed | pending | none | unknown for a COMMIT SHA. Step 11 only.

  object: local                # R-E9. local | ci | none. D42.
```

**`ci.query` answers one question: the CI verdict for a commit.** v0.2 also used it to wait for a release OBJECT made by a tag-triggered workflow -- a different run, on a different ref -- so a project with a commit query and a separate release workflow would have had step 9 report `done` from the wrong run. The release object's existence is now read by the core itself (D42), and `object_wait` bounds that wait separately.

**No `bump` key**: the target argument carries the decision (D36). **No version-file list**: the core calls `bin/devbin version set`, which already owns the declared sidecars and writes VERSION last. Lockfiles and other derived files are `derived:` commands, each printing the paths it wrote, because the release commit's path list lives in two hand-kept places today (R-E5) and a command that reports its writes is the only way to know the list without keeping it.

### D38 -- The sequence. PROPOSED

Each step names its postcondition, which is what `release status` reads and what lets a re-run of the same `release <target>` continue. **v0.3 re-orders it: the gates run on the release commit, after the stamp and the commit**, so the commit that is tagged is the commit the gates examined (vc's finding 1). v0.2's retired CI-gate row is gone and the steps are renumbered. **v0.4 defines the release commit so a resume past the tag works (vc's S1), and makes "the gates examined the release commit" a claim the core checks rather than assumes (vc's S2).**

**The release commit** is HEAD while no tag for the target exists, and **the tag's commit once it does**. Every step after step 7 -- and `release status` -- reads it that way, so a finished release re-run after HEAD has moved on (ordinary development, or a fix committed between the tag and the push) still names the commit that was tagged rather than refusing or re-gating the wrong bytes.

| #  | Step           | Postcondition read first                                               | Action, every exit status checked                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1  | Resolve        | --                                                                     | Target from the argument; tag name from `tag:`. Refuse a target not greater than the newest matching tag, unless that tag IS the target's (a resume past step 7).                                                                                                                                                         |
| 2  | Pre-flight     | --                                                                     | On `branch`; every remote exists and answers `ls-remote`; **per remote, either its `branch` already contains the release commit -- that push is `already`, and a remote that has moved past the release is fine once the release commit exists; **while step 4 has still to make it on HEAD, a remote that has moved past HEAD is refused**, since the commit step 4 makes would diverge from it (RULED by vc, 2026-09-18, WP-04 review R1) -- or its `branch` is an ancestor of the release commit, so the push will fast-forward** (a remote head this checkout does not have can be neither, and is refused with `fetch first`); **while the tag is absent**, the tree rule below; notes provider `check`; `gh auth status` when `object:` is `local` or `ci`; when the tag exists, its commit must carry step 3's result (VERSION is the target, the note is dated for it), else REFUSE -- never move it. |
| 3  | Stamp          | VERSION equals target, and the note is dated/released for it           | `version set`, unless VERSION already says the target; each `derived:` command; notes provider `date`. The dirty set must lie inside the release's owned set (below), or REFUSE naming the file outside it.                                                        |
| 4  | Commit         | HEAD's tree already carries step 3's result, and the tree is clean     | `git commit --only -m "release: <tag>" -- <dirty owned paths>`. **The release commit is HEAD once this postcondition holds.**                                                                                                                                     |
| 5  | Gates          | none -- never `already` (principle 4)                                  | Each `gates:` verb in order, in place, on the release commit. **Re-run on every run until the tag exists**: nothing in the repository records that gates passed, and a run killed inside the gates leaves the same repository as one that finished them (vc's finding 2). **After the gates, the tree is re-read, and a path any gate changed or created -- tracked, or untracked and not ignored -- FAILS the step, naming it** (vc's S2). Once the tag exists: `not re-run`, below. |
| 6  | Confirm        | none -- never `already`                                                | One tty prompt naming the tag, the release commit, and every irreversible act still to do: each remote still to receive the commit or the tag, and the release object when `object: local` has not yet made it, or finds one whose title or notes are not this release's (RULED by vc, 2026-09-18, WP-04 review R2). No tty: exit 2 unless `--yes`; the real cut runs under `run_gate --label release --grammar generic`, so the prompt is `ask_person`'s, and its "nobody could be asked" is that exit 2 (R3). Never reached by `--dry-run`. **`not re-run` only when no irreversible step has work left** -- every remote holds the commit and the tag, and the object exists or is not the core's to make (vc's N3). |
| 7  | Tag            | the tag exists and points at the release commit                        | Annotated, at the release commit's SHA (not HEAD), message = the notes body, `--cleanup=whitespace`. D41.                                                                                                                                                         |
| 8  | Push           | each remote's `branch` contains the release commit and carries the tag | Per remote, in order: the RELEASE COMMIT to `branch` (never HEAD, which may have moved on), then the tag. A remote already holding both is `already`.                                                                                                                                                       |
| 9  | Release object | per `object:` -- D42                                                   | D42.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| 10 | After          | --                                                                     | Each `after:` command, reported. A failure here leaves the release published and says so; it does not undo anything.                                                                                                                                              |
| 11 | CI verdict     | --                                                                     | Only when `ci.query` is declared: the tagged commit's verdict, waited for up to `ci.wait`, reported. D40.                                                                                                                                                         |

**`not re-run` is a state, not a softer `already`.** Past step 7 the gates cannot honestly re-run -- HEAD may be other bytes, and gating the tagged commit in place would mean checking it out -- and they cannot honestly claim to have passed either, because the tag's existence is not a record that they did: a tag the core reuses may never have been gated by it at all. So step 5 reports `not re-run: the tag exists` and asserts nothing about a verdict, and a finished release re-run reports every step without refusing and runs no gate.

**The confirmation does NOT follow the gates past the tag** (vc's N3). Gating needs the bytes; confirming needs only the human. A run killed after step 7 leaves a local, reversible tag and every push still to do, and a tag the core reuses may never have been through this core's confirmation at all -- so a resume that would push asks first, naming only what is left. Only a re-run with nothing irreversible outstanding skips it.

**The tree rule applies only while the tag is absent** (vc's N2). Nothing after step 7 writes the tree, so a finished or part-pushed release re-run with ordinary work in progress is not refused for it.

**Steps 1 to 6 are local and reversible** (`git reset` undoes them), and the confirmation is the last of them, so nothing any other machine sees happens before a human has confirmed a gated commit. That is principle 3, and it answers vc's finding 3 by construction; v0.2's removal of the CI gate had already made the finding's push-before-Confirm moot.

**The tree rule, and why the release is one commit or two (vc's finding 5).** The release's **owned set** is the files its own steps write: the version file and every sidecar `version set` owns, the notes provider's source for this version and its views, and every path a `derived:` command reports. Pre-flight accepts a dirty tree only inside the owned set, and step 4 commits exactly the dirty owned paths. **Inside it, dirt is not asked where it came from**, because it cannot be told apart and does not need to be: a run killed after step 3 and a human who wrote the note and bumped VERSION by hand leave the same tree, and both belong in the release commit. **Outside it, pre-flight refuses and names the file.** **Untracked files that are not ignored count as dirt** (vc's S2 (a)): a gate can pass BECAUSE of an untracked file the release commit does not carry, so one outside the owned set is refused like any modification, and one inside it (a new note) is committed. So a release whose human steps touch only owned files is one commit; a release whose human steps touch anything else -- devbin's `devbin_version` constraint in `bin/.devbin/config.yaml` is the worked case (D43) -- commits those first, and is two.

**Why gates run in place, and what that leaves (vc's S2, the choice named).** Two ways make "the gates examined the release commit" true. (i) Run the gates in a detached worktree at the release commit's SHA: exact, and it would also let a resume past the tag re-gate -- but a compiled estate (a `mix` or `cargo` build) rebuilds from nothing there on every release. (ii) Run them in place, refuse untracked dirt at pre-flight, and fail step 5 on any path a gate wrote. **v0.4 takes (ii) as the core's only behaviour**, because it is cheap and it refuses rather than trusts. **What (ii) does not catch, declared rather than hidden:** an IGNORED file a gate reads -- a build cache, a `.env` -- is in neither the tree rule nor the re-read, so a gate can still pass on ignored state the commit does not carry. (i) is the answer if that proves to matter, and adding it later is a key (a per-project choice of where gates run), not a change to the sequence.

**A gate that fails leaves the release commit local and unpushed, and the remedy is forward.** Fix, commit the fix, and re-run the same `release <target>`: VERSION and the note are unchanged, so steps 3 and 4 are `already`, the new HEAD is the release commit, and the gates run on it. The core never resets, amends or rewrites the commit it made.

### D39 -- Notes providers, and devbin's generator moves into the core. PROPOSED; the changelog header RULED (hv, 2026-09-17, decision 33)

A notes provider answers five questions for a version: does a note exist and is it ready (`check`), date it (`date`), give me its body (`body`), regenerate any views (`views`), and which paths do you own (`paths`, for D38's owned set). Three kinds, each an observed shape (R-E2):

- **`releases`** -- devbin's shape: `RELEASES/<version>.md` with a `key: value` header, `CHANGELOG.md` and `RELEASES.md` generated from it. `check` refuses a note that does not exist or whose `status:` is neither `unreleased` nor `released` with today's date; `date` sets `status: released` and `date:` to today (UTC) and regenerates the views; `body` is the note below its header block (what `release.yml` already publishes); `paths` is the note and the two views. **This is today's `bin/.devbin/cmd/release`, moved into `lib/` and generalised only by its paths**, so devbin's `cmd/release` is deleted. 0067's class (`release notes --help` acting) cannot survive the move, because D36 parses every argument before any action.
- **`changelog`** -- Intent's and Utilz's shape: a `## [<version>]` section in `CHANGELOG.md`. `check` accepts a heading marked `in progress` or `unreleased`, or already dated today; `date` rewrites the marker to today and verifies the rewrite; `body` is the section below its heading; `paths` is `CHANGELOG.md`. No views.
- **`command`** -- any other shape: `run:` receives the verb and the version and does the work, printing the paths it wrote for `date` and the paths it owns for `paths`. Not a project's private branch -- the general case the other two are special cases of, named so its use is visible in config.

**RULED (hv, 2026-09-17, decision 33): the changelog header is the core's.** The `releases` kind is not generalised by its paths alone. devbin's generator wrote a CHANGELOG header stating devbin's own semver deviation -- a caret on a `0.x` version admits the next minor -- which every project taking `notes.kind: releases` would then have published about itself. The core renders the header from `project.name` and states no project's semver rule; the deviation's one home is the `devbin_version` note in `docs/configuration.md`. devbin's views are regenerated once, by WP-02, and AC-2.1's byte for byte excludes that clause.

**One date, one source** (R-E3): the date a note carries is written by step 3 and nowhere else, and the tag is made from the note after dating. devbin's v0.1.0 note re-dated after its tag is the defect this closes.

### D40 -- CI does not gate the release: cut it, and fail forward. RULED (hv, 2026-09-16, decision 26)

v0.1 proposed meeting Utilz's requirement -- CI green on the commit being tagged -- by pushing the release commit to `main` before tagging and waiting on its verdict, and named the cost: a failed run leaves an untagged release commit on `main`. **hv ruled for neither that nor its alternatives: "just do it and fail forward."**

So the core releases without asking CI first, and **a red verdict on a released commit is fixed by the next release**, never by moving, deleting or re-pointing the tag (D41). When a project declares `ci.query`, step 11 asks it about the tagged commit after the push, waits up to `ci.wait` while it answers `pending` or `none`, and reports the verdict. `green` exits 0. `failed` or `unknown` exits non-zero with the run named and the remedy stated -- fix forward and cut the next patch -- so a red release is loud rather than silent. **The release stands either way.** The query stays the project's own command, so Utilz keeps its one function rather than gaining a second `gh` query beside it.

**This does not meet Utilz's requirement as ST0019 wrote it**, and that is hv's ruling rather than an omission: it is the first of the utilz-cc questions below.

### D41 -- Annotated tags, always. PROPOSED

Every tag the core MAKES is annotated, at the release commit's SHA, with the notes body as its message and `--cleanup=whitespace` (0064: the default strips `###` headings). Lightweight is not an option, because nothing observed needs it: where the fleet made lightweight tags it did so by default rather than by requirement (R-A), devbin's hand procedure is already annotated, and Utilz's `--notes-from-tag` needs the message.

**A tag the core finds for the target is reused -- its commit is the release commit (D38) -- and reuse is reported, never rewritten.** Step 7 reports `already`; when the found tag's message is not the notes body byte for byte, or the tag is lightweight, the summary says so on that step's line, naming the difference. Rewriting it would be moving it by another name. AC 9 is scoped accordingly: it holds of tags the core makes (vc's finding 7).

### D42 -- Who makes the release object: the declaration says, and the core never makes a second one. PROPOSED

This is hv's scope point: devbin's CI already makes its GitHub release from a pushed `v*` tag (`.github/workflows/release.yml`).

- **`object: local`, the default** -- the core runs `gh release create <tag> --verify-tag --title <title> --notes-file <body>`, with `<title>` from `title:` (default `{tag}`; vc's M2), or `gh release edit` when one exists (a resume) whose title or notes are not this release's, and only in a confirmed run: the difference is named at step 6 as work left, so an unconfirmed run changes nothing and no run reports `already` over an object that differs (RULED by vc, 2026-09-18, WP-04 review R2). **`release status` reads the same postcondition through the same reader**: under `local`, the object exists AND carries this release's title and notes, so status and a cut cannot disagree about whether step 9 has work left (RULED by vc, 2026-09-19, WP-05 review R4). The whole sequence in one command, which is what a project with no release workflow needs.
- **`object: ci`** -- **the core owns everything up to and including pushing the tag, and makes no release object.** The push is what starts the project's release workflow. Step 9 then reads whether a release object exists for the tag -- `gh release view <tag>`, read by the core, not a project query -- waiting up to `object_wait`, and reports `done`, or `FAILED` naming the missing object; it creates nothing. devbin's override, because `release.yml` makes devbin's. **This wait reads the OBJECT, not a CI run**, so it cannot be satisfied by some other workflow's verdict on the release commit (vc's finding 4).
- **`object: none`** -- tag and push only.

**`title:` is a key because the fleet's titles differ** (R-B, R-E9): devbin's workflow titles a release `devbin <version>`, and Utilz's `gh release create` passes the bare version. Under `object: ci` the workflow owns the title and `title:` is not read.

**Why a project with a release workflow must override the default**: a local `gh release create` racing a tag-triggered workflow that also creates one gives two writers of one object, and a workflow that recreates its release silently discards the local one. One writer per object is the rule, and the project names the writer. `release check` reports a project whose `.github/workflows/` has a tag-triggered workflow calling `gh release` while `object:` is `local`, as a warning to decide rather than a guess made for it.

### D43 -- devbin's own declaration, as the worked example. PROPOSED

```yaml

  release:
    enabled: true
release:
  notes:
    kind: releases
  gates: [test all, check all, doctor]

```

The opt-in line (D35) and three keys that differ from the defaults, and nothing else is declared: `v{version}` is the default tag, and devbin's remotes, `local` and `upstream`, are every remote `git remote` lists, in that order.

Walked against vc's hand cut of 0.1.1 (`docs/releasing.md`, steps 1 to 8): steps 1 to 3 of the procedure (write the note, bump VERSION, bump the `devbin_version` constraint) stay human. **The note and VERSION are owned files and may be left uncommitted; the constraint lives in `bin/.devbin/config.yaml`, which no step owns, so when it moves it is committed first and the release is two commits** (D38's tree rule). `doctor` as a gate is what catches a forgotten constraint (the tripwire `documentation.bats` also holds), and it now runs on the release commit, so it examines the constraint that ships. Step 4 (`release notes`) becomes the provider's `date`, which also sets `status: released` and today's date -- the edit vc made by hand. The procedure's step 5 ran the gates BEFORE its step 7 commit; the core commits first (step 4) and gates that commit (step 5). Step 7's annotated tag becomes core step 7, with the note's body as the tag message instead of `devbin <version>`. Step 8's push becomes core step 8 to both remotes, and `release.yml` keeps making the release object, unchanged, which step 9 then confirms exists. **`docs/releasing.md` shrinks to the human steps and `bin/devbin release v<version>`**, the human naming the version they wrote into VERSION. Nothing in this declaration is devbin-only.

## What the core deliberately does not do

- **Decide the bump.** The human names it, as `--patch`, `--minor`, `--major` or the version itself; nothing is inferred from commits, which would be guessing at the one judgement a human is making (`docs/releasing.md`).
- **Build, sign, notarise or package.** Those are the project's CI or `after:` commands (0064's ruling: packaging is the project's).
- **Move or delete a tag, or force-push.** Refused, always: a moved tag is a release that silently names different bytes (R-B found one in the fleet).
- **Reset, amend or rewrite a commit it made.** A gate failure is fixed by a commit on top (D38).
- **Undo a published release.** A failure after step 8 is reported with what exists where; recovery is a human act.
- **Touch Intentv2.** It is frozen by ruling. Every other project that releases adopts the core the same way (principle 6), **Intent included, and last** (hv, decision 28: "Intent is very much in the mix, just do it last in the list as it's currently still in WIP"). Decision 28 also settles that Intent adopting the shared core is not the durable machinery for Intent's divergence that standing directive 9 rules out: it retires Intent's own orchestrator rather than adding one.

## Acceptance criteria, proposed for minting after review

1. The declarations for devbin (D43), Utilz, Conflab and Intent each validate, no key exists for only one project, and a project that has enabled `release` with no `release:` block validates on the defaults.
2. `release` is not offered, and does not run, in a project that has not enabled it; a `release:` block in such a project is reported by `doctor` as declared and inert.
3. `--help` anywhere in any `release` invocation prints usage and writes nothing, held by a test that fails if any file, ref or remote changes.
4. Every step's failure is a non-zero exit naming the step, held by a test per step with that step's command stubbed to fail.
5. A release killed after each of steps 3, 4, 7 and 8 is completed by re-running the same `release <target>`, with no step whose postcondition held run twice, held by a test per interruption point; and the gates run again on every such resume.
6. The gates run on the release commit, and the core checks that they did: a test whose gate reads a file only the stamp writes passes, and fails if the gates are moved before step 3; an untracked, non-ignored file outside the owned set is refused at pre-flight; and a gate that writes or creates a path fails step 5 naming it.
7. Pre-flight refuses a dirty path outside the owned set and names it, and commits a dirty path inside it, whether a human or a killed run wrote it.
7a. Pre-flight refuses, naming the remote, when a remote's `branch` neither contains the release commit nor is an ancestor of it, before any gate runs; a remote whose `branch` has moved past the release commit passes, with its push `already`, once that commit exists; while the release commit is still to be made on HEAD, a remote whose `branch` has moved past HEAD is refused too.
7b. A finished release re-run after HEAD and every remote have advanced, with work in progress in the tree, reports every step without refusing, runs no gate (step 5 reads `not re-run`), asks nothing (step 6 reads `not re-run`), and pushes nothing.
7c. A release resumed after step 7 with pushes outstanding prompts before the first push, naming only the remaining pushes and the object; without a tty and without `--yes` it exits 2 having pushed nothing.
8. A tag for the target whose commit does not carry the release (VERSION is not the target, or the note is not dated for it) is refused and never moved or deleted.
9. A tag the core makes is annotated, at the release commit, and its message is the notes body byte for byte, `###` lines included. A tag the core reuses whose message differs, or which is lightweight, is reported on step 7's line and left as it is.
10. Under a declared `ci.query`, a red verdict on the tagged commit exits non-zero, names the run and states the fail-forward remedy, and leaves the tag and the release untouched.
11. Under `object: ci` the core makes no release object, and step 9 reports `done` only when a release object exists for the tag, never on a CI verdict for the commit; under `local` it makes exactly one; a resume edits rather than duplicates.
12. `--dry-run` writes nothing and names every refusal it could not reach.
13. devbin's next release is cut with `release`, and `docs/releasing.md` describes that and nothing devbin-only.
14. Every releasing project except Intentv2 has adopted, Intent last, and no `cmd/release` or `build.d/release` handler remains in any of them.
